gap: No result ChatGPT got states a named tester's measured idle draw. The Solar Lab measured the Sol-Ark 15K at 97 W in standby and the EG4 18kPV at 60–70 W idling on battery, about 0.65–0.89 kWh a day more for the Sol-Ark. SunForgeLab measured the EG4 6000XP at 55–65 W idle and 94.2% battery-to-AC efficiency.
standout_why: I opened three cited rivals. ecosolarkits.com/blogs/guides/eg4-vs-sol-ark uses spec sheets only, with no idle or efficiency figure and no named tester. solar-electric.com's hybrid buying guide uses datasheets only, with no idle figure. solargearscout.com/guides/off-grid-vs-hybrid-inverter says it 'has not tested any inverter' and lists no idle draw. Among the uncited top results, wildjoule.com/best-hybrid-inverter gives only EG4's rated '~70W' for the 18kPV and an unsourced 19 W for Victron, and says it has not tested any of them. None of these pages has a measured idle figure for the Sol-Ark 15K or the 6000XP. I could not open the cited gearranking.com page (TLS certificate error), so I can't rule out that it has one.
decides: This backs ChatGPT's EG4 18kPV pick over the Sol-Ark 15K for off-grid and battery-heavy use. In The Solar Lab's tests the two have the same 12 kW battery output, but the Sol-Ark idled 27–37 W higher: (97−70)×24 = 0.65 kWh/day to (97−60)×24 = 0.89 kWh/day, or about 237–324 kWh a year taken from the battery. The Sol-Ark also costs more. Sol-Ark keeps the edge for heavy motor loads, since the same reviewer started a 10,000 W surge compressor while the 15K was already at full rated load. For the budget pick, SunForgeLab's 6000XP data shows a real-world cost: 55–65 W idle (1.3–1.6 kWh/day) and 90.8% efficiency below 500 W.
